principles: A short charge to a son already doing well
Praying the opposite of the Rameumptom

world_behind.title: Shiblon went to Antionum
world_behind.text: Alma 31:7 named him among those Alma took to the Zoramites. Verses 3 and 4 refer to what happened to him there, and the record gives that history only here.

world_behind.title: He was jailed and stoned
world_behind.text: Verse 4 says he was in bonds and stoned for the word's sake. Nothing in Alma 31 through 35 mentions it; Alma supplies the detail privately to the son it happened to.

world_behind.title: This is the shortest of the three charges
world_behind.text: Fifteen verses, against thirty for Helaman's first and forty-seven for his second. Alma has less to correct and says so.

world_behind.title: The conversion account is compressed
world_behind.text: Verses 7 and 8 give the angel, the three days, and the cry for mercy in two verses. Alma 36 spent twenty-four on the same material.

world_behind.title: The Zoramite prayer is still in view
world_behind.text: Verses 13 and 14 tell Shiblon how not to pray, using the Rameumptom as the example. He was standing there when it was offered.

world_behind.title: The instructions are mostly about restraint
world_behind.text: Not lifted up, not boasting, not overbearing, bridle the passions, refrain from idleness. The list is almost entirely about what to hold back.

world_behind.title: The farewell matches Helaman's
world_behind.text: Verse 15 ends with teaching the word, being sober, and farewell, the same three items that close Alma 37.

words.text: Constancy, holding a course. The word appears four times in this record and never in the King James Bible. Alma names it first among Shiblon's qualities, and Alma 39 opens by asking Corianton whether he has observed the steadiness of his brother.

Acute distress of body or mind. It appears eleven times in the record, and the King James Bible seventeen. Alma pairs it with bitter pain to cover three days in one phrase, where Alma 36 needed six verses.

Moderate, self-restrained. The record uses it twice and the King James Bible three times, always in lists of qualities expected of a teacher. Alma 7:23 has the same word in a longer list Alma gave publicly at Gideon.
Domineering force in speech or manner. The word occurs once in scripture. Alma pairs it against boldness in the same clause, which makes it the excess of a quality he is asking his son to keep.

To fit with a bridle, to control as a horse is controlled. The word turns up once here, and the King James Bible nine times, including James on bridling the whole body. Alma applies it to the passions and attaches a purpose: that ye may be filled with love.
The state of not deserving. Three uses here, with none in the King James Bible. Alma makes acknowledging it the substance of the prayer he wants, in place of the thanksgiving the Zoramites offered.

phrases.term: Even as I said unto Helaman
phrases.text: Alma opens by telling one son what he told the other. The promise is identical to Alma 36:1 and 37:13, and he repeats it word for word so that Shiblon knows the family standard is the same.

phrases.term: Blessed is he that endureth to the end
phrases.text: Alma's hope for a son who has already started well. He credits Shiblon with commencing in his youth and puts the blessing on continuing.

phrases.term: I also know that thou wast stoned for the word's sake
phrases.text: The one place the record mentions this. Alma names it, says his son bore it with patience, and credits the Lord with the deliverance, without describing anything further.

phrases.term: As much as ye shall put your trust in God even so much ye shall be delivered
phrases.text: A proportional promise. Alma states the relation as a measure, and applies it to trials, troubles, and afflictions in that order.

phrases.term: I did cry unto him and I did find peace to my soul
phrases.text: The conversion in ten words. Alma 36 gave the same event at length; here the cry and the peace sit in one clause, and verse 9 says why he is telling it.

phrases.term: There is no other way or means whereby man can be saved, only in and through Christ
phrases.text: The reason Alma gives for retelling his own story. Nephi says the same in 2 Nephi 31:21 and Peter says it before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4:12), and Alma offers it as the lesson the story exists to carry.
Six words containing the chapter's method. Alma keeps the quality and names its excess, which is how the rest of the verse works too: passions bridled so that love can fill, idleness refused.

phrases.term: See that ye bridle all your passions, that ye may be filled with love
phrases.text: The restraint has a stated purpose. Alma does not ask for passions to be removed; the bridling is what makes room for something else.

phrases.term: Do not pray as the Zoramites do, for ye have seen that they pray to be heard of men
phrases.text: Alma appeals to something his son witnessed. Shiblon stood at Antionum and watched the Rameumptom, and the instruction is built on that memory.

phrases.term: O Lord, forgive my unworthiness, and remember my brethren in mercy
phrases.text: The prayer Alma supplies in place of the Zoramite one. It reverses both halves: unworthiness for chosenness, and mercy for the brethren in place of thanks that they are damned.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: A formula the speaker marks as a repeat
verses.text: The chapter opens by quoting the speaker's own earlier words and saying so: "even as I said unto Helaman, that inasmuch as ye shall keep the commandments of God ye shall prosper in the land." Nine verses of the volume carry that clause, and three of them are Alma saying it to a son, at Alma 36:1, Alma 37:13 and here. The reader is told the sentence is second-hand before it is used, so the address to Shiblon begins by being explicitly the same address given to his brother.

verses.label: v. 3–4
verses.title: A biography that exists only in this aside
verses.text: The father's praise is specific and evidential: "I know that thou wast in bonds; yea, and I also know that thou wast stoned for the word's sake; and thou didst bear all these things with patience." Shiblon is named in thirteen verses of the volume, and this is the only one that reports either the imprisonment or the stoning. Alma 31:7 has him going out to the Zoramites; nothing narrates what happened there. An episode that would be a chapter for anyone else survives as a subordinate clause inside a compliment.

verses.label: v. 6–9
verses.title: The conversion, told a third time and shortened
verses.text: The record carries Alma's account of his own conversion three times. This is the briefest, three verses, and the only one prefaced by a warning about how the speaker knows anything: "I would not that ye should think that I know these things of myself, but it is the Spirit of God which is in me." The three days are reported as "three days and three nights in the most bitter pain and anguish of soul," and the turning point is compressed to a single clause, "never, until I did cry out unto the Lord Jesus Christ for mercy."

verses.label: v. 10–12
verses.title: The register changes to command and stays there
verses.text: After nine verses of testimony, three verses of imperatives arrive with no transition: continue to teach, be diligent and temperate, see that ye are not lifted up, do not boast, use boldness but not overbearance, bridle all your passions, refrain from idleness. Several are stated as balanced pairs rather than single prohibitions. Bridle occurs once in the volume, in verse 12, and the metaphor is not explained anywhere.

verses.label: v. 13
verses.title: A negative example the reader has already seen
verses.text: The instruction names a group and expects recognition: "Do not pray as the Zoramites do, for ye have seen that they pray to be heard of men, and to be praised for their wisdom." Ye have seen is doing real work, because Shiblon was there. Alma 31:7 lists him among the party, and Alma 31:15–18 preserves the prayer in full. The counsel does not describe the fault; it points seven chapters back and lets the quoted text supply it.

verses.label: v. 14
verses.title: Two prayers, in the shape of a parable told elsewhere
verses.text: The verse gives a wrong prayer and a right one: "Do not say: O God, I thank thee that we are better than our brethren; but rather say: O Lord, forgive my unworthiness, and remember my brethren in mercy." Luke 18:11 and 18:13 set the same two prayers side by side, where the Pharisee says "God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are" and the publican says "God be merciful to me a sinner." The Gospel makes it a story with two characters. Here it is an instruction to one man, with both prayers put in his own mouth.

verses.label: v. 15
verses.title: The same two words that closed the last address
verses.text: The blessing ends the chapter and the last command in it is the shortest: "Now go, my son, and teach the word unto this people. Be sober." Be sober stands in two verses of the volume. The other is Alma 37:47, the closing line of the counsel to Helaman one chapter earlier. Two consecutive addresses to two sons end on the identical two words, which is checkable in a way that no reading of the tone can be.

chapter.title: The shortest charge goes to the son doing best
chapter.text: Fifteen verses, and most of them are commendation and general instruction. Alma spends his length where it is needed, and Alma 39 shows where that is.

chapter.title: A son's suffering is on the record only because his father named it
chapter.text: Bonds and stoning at Antionum appear nowhere in the mission account. The private charge is where it is preserved.

chapter.title: The conversion is retold as an argument
chapter.text: Verse 9 says why: so Shiblon may learn that salvation comes through Christ alone. The story is offered as evidence rather than as memoir.

chapter.title: The virtues are named with their excesses
chapter.text: Verse 12 gives three instructions and two of them are stated as limits on a good thing: "Use boldness, but not overbearance," "bridle all your passions," and "refrain from idleness." Verse 11 has already done the same with wisdom and strength, "see that ye do not boast in your own wisdom, nor of your much strength." Four qualities in two verses, each named with the edge marked, so the son is given a test rather than a virtue.

chapter.title: Bridling is for filling
chapter.text: The clause at verse 12 is "bridle all your passions, that ye may be filled with love." The restraint is given a purpose and the purpose is capacity, not merit. Nothing else in these books uses the verb "bridle" of a person, and the sentence supplies the only stated reason for the restraint anywhere in the chapter.

chapter.title: The counter-prayer is exact
chapter.text: Verse 13 names the model to avoid, "Do not pray as the Zoramites do," and verse 14 gives the two forms side by side: "Do not say: O God, I thank thee that we are better than our brethren; but rather say: O Lord, forgive my unworthiness, and remember my brethren in mercy." The prayer being reversed is quoted at Alma 31:17, which thanks God for election and for others "elected to be cast by thy wrath down to hell." Both of its clauses are inverted here, the self-comparison and the verdict on the brethren.

chapter.title: He cites what his son saw
chapter.text: Alma does not describe Zoramite worship. He says ye have seen, because Shiblon was there, and lets the memory carry the instruction.

chapter.title: The three charges share a closing
chapter.text: Teach the word, be sober, farewell. Alma 37 and Alma 38 end with the same three, which makes the difference in Alma 42's ending visible when it comes.

applications.title: Tell someone what you have noticed about them
applications.text: Alma lists four things by name, "thy faithfulness and thy diligence, and thy patience and thy long-suffering among the people of the Zoramites," and adds what he knows of the cost, that Shiblon was in bonds and stoned. Specific praise is worth more than the general kind, and it requires having paid attention.

applications.title: Say where your knowledge of them came from
applications.text: Alma adds a caveat to the praise, "I would not that ye should think that I know these things of myself." He is not claiming to have watched. When you tell somebody what you have seen in them, be honest about how you saw it.

applications.title: Give the useful part of your own history
applications.text: Alma tells the story in two verses and draws one lesson, "that ye may learn of me that there is no other way or means whereby man can be saved, only in and through Christ." The account is short and it is entirely instrumental.

applications.title: Keep the quality and name the excess
applications.text: "Use boldness, but not overbearance," and the same shape governs diligence against idleness. Teaching by marking the edge of a good quality lets a person tell when they have crossed it.

applications.title: Bridle rather than remove
applications.text: The purpose of the control is stated, "bridle all your passions, that ye may be filled with love." The restraint is presented as making room rather than as reducing you.

applications.title: Write the opposite prayer
applications.text: Alma gives his son the exact form to avoid and the exact form to use, "Do not say: O God, I thank thee that we are better than our brethren; but rather say: O Lord, forgive my unworthiness, and remember my brethren in mercy." Try writing out the version of your own prayer that inverts its comparisons.

applications.title: Attach a habit to the correction
applications.text: The instruction closes with "acknowledge your unworthiness before God at all times," which turns a one-off adjustment into a standing practice. A correction with no recurring form attached tends not to survive the week.

applications.title: Send them back to work
applications.text: The blessing ends with a job and two words of manner, "Now go, my son, and teach the word unto this people. Be sober." Praise that does not end in an assignment leaves the person nowhere to put it.

questions.text: What have I commenced in that I have not continued?
What have I borne patiently that nobody else knows about?
Have I trusted God in proportion to the deliverance I expect?
Could I say in a single line why I believe what I believe?
Where does my boldness turn into overbearance?
Whose approval am I actually praying toward?
When did I last ask God to remember someone else in mercy?
